interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a net force that appears only while the trolley's speed changes and vanishes while it runs steady, when you drag the corners of its speed graph.
interactive.title: The trolley and its two graphs
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: The picture runs over fifteen small screens. The main picture is a crane trolley on a level rail, with an example mass of 2000 kg. Above it is its speed-time graph. Speed runs up the side from 0 to 1 m/s. Time runs along the bottom from 0 to 16 s. Below that is its net force graph on the same time line. The speed graph opens as one run. The trolley speeds up from rest to 0.5 m/s in the first 2 s, runs steady until 6 s, then brakes to rest at 8 s. You drag the graph's corners. Up and down sets the top speed, from 0.1 to 1 m/s. Sideways sets when each part starts and ends. The speeding up and the braking can each last 1 to 6 s. On Play, the trolley runs along the rail. A marker runs along both graphs with it. Readouts give the speed in m/s, the acceleration in m/s² and the net force in N at the marker. On a narrow phone the three readouts wrap onto two lines. Two amber lines mark each sloping part of the speed graph, with no fill. They show the rise in speed and the time it took. The rise over the time is the acceleration. The area under the speed line is shaded too. Its label gives the distance covered so far, in metres. The net force is the mass times the acceleration. So the force graph sits flat at zero wherever the speed line is flat. It steps up or down only where the speed line slopes. In the opening run it reads +500 N for the first 2 s. That is 2000 × 0.25 m/s². It reads zero while the trolley runs steady and −500 N while it brakes. On the trolley, arrows show the drive's push or the brake, friction, and the net force. Friction is an example 100 N against the motion while the trolley moves. So the drive pushes 600 N while speeding up and 100 N while running steady. The brake adds 400 N while braking. A switch turns friction off. A button takes the push away during the steady run. With friction on, the speed line then slopes down at 0.05 m/s². That is 100 N ÷ 2000 kg. From the opening 0.5 m/s, the trolley stops 10 s and 2.5 m later. With friction off, nothing acts along the rail. The force graph stays at zero and the trolley rolls on at its speed to the end of the graph. A Couple up mode turns friction off. It rolls trolley A, 2000 kg at 0.5 m/s, into trolley B, 2000 kg at rest. The buffers press for an example 0.5 s. Meanwhile an arrow of 1000 N on each trolley points away from the other. The two arrows stay drawn afterwards, labelled while the buffers pressed, 0.5 s. A bar under each trolley shows its momentum in kg m/s. That is its mass × its speed. A's bar shrinks from 1000 to 500 as B's grows from 0 to 500. The coupled pair roll on at 0.25 m/s. A total bar stays at 1000 all the way. Screen 1 shows the opening run speeding up. The slope is 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 m/s². The triangle's area is ½ × 2 × 0.5 = 0.5 m. The steady part then adds 0.5 × 4 = 2 m. It names v = u + at, and says slope and area are the derivative and the integral. Screen 2 asks for the acceleration of a trolley that goes from rest to 0.6 m/s in 3 s. The answer is 0.2 m/s². One wrong pick is 5 m/s², the time ÷ the speed. The other is 0.9 m, the area, which is a distance. Screen 3 shows a speed line rising from 0.5 to 1 m/s over 2 s, at 0.25 m/s². Its area splits into a rectangle, ut = 0.5 × 2 = 1 m, and a triangle, ½at² = ½ × 0.25 × 2² = 0.5 m. That makes s = ut + ½at² = 1.5 m in all. Screen 4 asks how far a trolley at 0.4 m/s goes while braking steadily to rest in 4 s. The answer is 0.8 m. One wrong pick is 1.6 m, as if it kept its speed. The other is 0.1 m, the speed ÷ the time. Its working names s = ½(u + v)t. Screen 5 asks how far a trolley at 0.6 m/s goes while braking steadily at 0.2 m/s² to rest, with no time given. It uses v² = u² + 2as. The answer is 0.36 ÷ 0.4 = 0.9 m. One wrong pick is 1.8 m, with the 2 left out. The other is 1.5 m, with the speed not squared. The trolley sits on a rail marked in metres, and the right answer draws it at rest 0.9 m along. Screen 6 takes the push away during the steady run, first with friction on and then with it off. Screen 7 shows the trolley running steady at 0.5 m/s, with its drive and friction arrows. It asks which statement is true. The right pick is that the push equals friction, so the net force is zero. One wrong pick says the push must be bigger than friction to keep it moving. The other says no force acts on it at all. Screen 8 plays the opening run with its force graph: +500 N, then zero, then −500 N. Screen 9 asks for the acceleration of the 2000 kg trolley when its drive pushes 600 N against 100 N of friction. The answer is 0.25 m/s². One wrong pick is 0.3 m/s², the push alone ÷ the mass. The other is 0.35 m/s², from adding the push and friction. Screen 10 shades the area under the force graph while the trolley speeds up. That area is 500 N × 2 s = 1000 N s. That is mass × acceleration × time, which is mass × the change in speed. The trolley's momentum grows to 2000 × 0.5 = 1000 kg m/s. Beside it, a small beam turns about a pivot. Its label says a moment is not momentum. It is a turning effect, force × distance, in N m. Screen 11 asks for the momentum of a 1500 kg trolley at 0.4 m/s. The answer is 600 kg m/s. One wrong pick is 600 N m, which has a moment's unit. The other is 3750 kg m/s, the mass ÷ the speed. Screen 12 plays Couple up. Each buffer gives an impulse of 1000 N × 0.5 s = 500 N s. The pair share 1000 ÷ 4000 = 0.25 m/s. Screens 13 to 15 mix it all. Screen 13 asks how hard B pushes on A while A pushes B with 1000 N. The answer is 1000 N backwards. One wrong pick is no push at all, as if B only gets pushed. The other is 500 N backwards, as if a still trolley pushes less. Screen 14 asks for the shared speed when a 1000 kg trolley at 0.8 m/s couples to a still 3000 kg trolley. The answer is 0.2 m/s. One wrong pick is 0.4 m/s, half the speed, as if the masses were equal. The other is 0.8 m/s, as if it kept its speed. Screen 15 asks for the net force on a 2000 kg trolley whose speed rises from 0.2 to 0.8 m/s in 4 s. The answer is 300 N. One wrong pick is 400 N, from the end speed instead of the change. The other is 1200 N, the mass × the change in speed with no time. From screen 8 on, a caption under the picture says the force graph follows the slope of the speed graph. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. A wrong pick is drawn so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The trolley is one solid body on a level rail. Its wheels' own spin, the rail's slope and any swing of a hanging load are left out. Friction is drawn as an example: one steady 100 N while it moves. Real rolling resistance grows with the load and changes a little with speed. Each part of the run is drawn with a steady acceleration, so the speed graph is made of straight lines. A real drive and brake ease in and out, so the corners are rounded. In Couple up, the buffers' push is drawn as steady for 0.5 s. A real buffer's push rises and falls. The momentum it moves still sets the area under it. So the shared speed is the same. Air drag is left out too. At a trolley's walking pace it is tiny next to rolling friction. But a fast body slows from it even on a perfect rail.

explain.text:
A moving thing needs no net force to keep it moving. A net force changes how it moves. With no net force, a moving trolley rolls on at a steady speed in a straight line, and a still one stays still.[^1] A net force speeds it up or slows it down. Velocity has a direction too, so a net force across the motion turns it. Plot speed against time. The slope of that line is the acceleration. It tells you how fast the speed changes, in m/s². The area under the line is the distance covered. Take a crane trolley that speeds up from rest to 0.5 m/s in 2 s. Its slope is 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 m/s². The area under that part is a triangle: ½ × 2 × 0.5 = 0.5 m. For a steady acceleration, the slope and the area give four handy equations. Call the start speed u, the end speed v, the acceleration a, the time t and the distance s. The slope gives v = u + at. The area is the average speed times the time, so s = ½(u + v)t. Split the area into a rectangle and a triangle to get s = ut + ½at². The first gives t = (v − u) ÷ a. Put that into s = ½(u + v)t. Then s = (v + u)(v − u) ÷ 2a = (v² − u²) ÷ 2a. That rearranges to v² = u² + 2as.

Push a loaded trolley and let go, and it slows down and stops. That is why it feels as if motion needs a force. But a force did act. Friction held it back. Take away friction and air drag on a level rail, and nothing would slow it. It would roll on at the same speed. Add up every force on a body, as on a free-body diagram. What is left is the [[net force]]. A body moving at a steady velocity has no net force on it.[^2] A hook hanging still has forces that add to nothing. A trolley rolling at a steady 0.5 m/s along a straight rail is in balance in just the same way. Its drive pushes it forward exactly as hard as friction holds it back.

A net force changes the velocity, and a change in velocity is an acceleration.[^3] The acceleration is in proportion to the net force and in its direction.[^4] The same force gives a heavier body less acceleration, in inverse proportion to its mass. Put together, net force = mass × acceleration, or F = ma. F is in newtons, m in kilograms and a in m/s². The 2000 kg trolley gaining 0.5 m/s in 2 s needs 2000 × 0.25 = 500 N net. If friction holds it back with 100 N, its drive must push 600 N. Running steady, the drive pushes just 100 N, and the net force is zero. Braking to rest in 2 s takes 500 N net the other way. So a graph of net force against time is not a copy of the speed graph. It follows the speed graph's slope. On a straight rail it is zero wherever the speed is steady. The size of that speed makes no difference.

For a steady net force acting for a time t, the acceleration is the change in speed ÷ t. So F × t = m × the change in speed. Mass × velocity is a body's [[momentum]], in kg m/s. Force × time is the [[impulse]]. It is the area under the force graph. A newton is a kg m/s², so a newton second is the same unit as a kg m/s. The 500 N net push for 2 s is 1000 N s. It gives the trolley 2000 × 0.5 = 1000 kg m/s of momentum. Momentum is not a moment. A moment is a turning effect, in newton metres. Newton's third law says forces come in pairs. When one body pushes on another, the other pushes back just as hard, the opposite way. So when a moving trolley couples to a still one, each pushes the other equally, for the same time. One loses as much momentum as the other gains. So the total stays the same, as long as nothing else pushes along the rail. A 2000 kg trolley at 0.5 m/s carries 1000 kg m/s. Couple it to a still 2000 kg trolley, and 4000 kg share that momentum. So the pair roll on at 0.25 m/s. Here each trolley is one solid body on a level rail. That is a simplified case. Real trolleys also have wheels that spin, rails that may slope, and air drag. **A moving thing needs no net force to keep moving. A net force changes its velocity, and net force = mass × acceleration.**

analogy.text: Think of an inductor. It behaves like a mass. In an ideal coil, a steady current flows on with no voltage across it. A voltage does not set the current. It sets how fast the current changes. The voltage is the inductance × the rate of change of current. A net force does the same to a trolley's speed. The force is the mass × the rate of change of speed. The bigger the inductance, the slower the current changes, just as a heavier trolley speeds up more slowly.
analogy.breaks: A real coil has resistance. With no voltage its current dies away, much as friction stops a real trolley. And a single coil has no twin of the third law. Nothing in it pushes back on a second body.

practice.text:
- Safe way first: never try to stop a moving trolley or load with your hands or body. Only a force acting over time removes its momentum. The shorter the time, the bigger the force. Stopping 2000 kg at 0.5 m/s in half a second takes 2000 N on average.
- Sketch the speed-time graph. Mark the start speed, the end speed and the time of each part.
- Find each part's acceleration from its slope: the change in speed ÷ the time.
- Find the distance from the area under the line. Or use the equation that fits the three things you know.
- Draw the free-body diagram and add the forces along the motion. That sum is the net force.
- Set the net force equal to mass × acceleration. A drive must give the net force plus whatever friction takes.
- Where two bodies push only on each other along a line, the momentum before equals the momentum after.

**Rule of thumb:** steady speed in a straight line means zero net force, whatever the speed. The net force sets how fast the speed changes, not the speed itself.

**Worked example:** take an example crane trolley of 2000 kg. It must reach 0.5 m/s in 2 s against 100 N of friction. Its acceleration is 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 m/s². The net force is 2000 × 0.25 = 500 N. So the drive pushes 500 + 100 = 600 N. It covers ½ × 2 × 0.5 = 0.5 m while it speeds up. Once at speed, the drive needs only 100 N. To stop in 2 s it needs 500 N backwards. Friction gives 100 N of that. So the brake gives 400 N.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking a moving thing needs a push to keep going. It needs one only to make up for friction, drag or a slope.
- Using the drive's push in F = ma instead of the net force.
- Reading the area under a speed graph as the acceleration, or its slope as the distance.
- Forgetting the pair: when A pushes B, B pushes A back just as hard.
- Calling momentum a moment. Momentum is mass × velocity, in kg m/s. A moment is force × distance, in N m.

interactive.html:
A crane trolley on a level rail, with an example mass of 2000 kg and an example 100 N of friction while it moves. The other trolleys, speeds and times are examples too.

Net force = mass × acceleration, so the force graph follows the slope of the speed graph, not its height.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a net force that appears only while the trolley's speed changes and vanishes while it runs steady, when you drag the corners of its speed graph.

checks.label: The opening run: at 1 s the speed is 0.25 m/s, the acceleration 0.25 m/s² and the net force 500 N; at 4 s it is 0.5 m/s with none; at 7 s it is 0.25 m/s, −0.25 m/s² and −500 N
The area is the distance: 0.5 m by 2 s, 2.5 m by 6 s, 3 m by 8 s; screen 3 splits 1.5 m into a 1 m rectangle and a 0.5 m triangle, the same as the average speed times the time
Summed in thin strips, the area under the speed line matches the distance the trolley is drawn at, for every corner setting
The force graph follows the slope: measured from the speed line itself, the net force is the mass times its slope at every moment and every corner setting

Any object moving at constant velocity has no net external force acting upon it: wherever the speed line is flat, at every top speed, the net force is zero, the force graph drawn sits on its zero line and no net force arrow is drawn

The acceleration of a system is directly proportional to and in the same direction as the net external force: at every corner setting and moment, the net force read is the mass times the acceleration, with the same sign

A body in motion remains in motion at constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force: with the push gone and friction off, the trolley keeps its speed to the end of the graph with no net force; with friction on, it slows and stops
With the push gone and friction on, the speed falls at 100 ÷ 2000 = 0.05 m/s², so the trolley stops 10 s and 2.5 m later

The drive gives the net force plus friction: 600 N while speeding up and 100 N while running steady; braking, the brake gives 400 N and friction 100 N; the drive arrow drawn is longer while speeding up
Couple up: each buffer pushes 1000 N for 0.5 s; A's momentum falls from 1000 to 500 kg m/s as B's rises from 0 to 500, the total stays 1000 at every moment, and the pair roll on at 0.25 m/s

The worked numbers: 0.25 m/s², 0.5 m and 2 m; 0.2, 5 and 0.9; 1 m, 0.5 m and 1.5 m; 0.8, 1.6 and 0.1 m; 0.36, 0.9, 1.8 and 1.5 m; 500 N s each in the coupling; 500, 600 and 400 N; 0.25, 0.3 and 0.35 m/s²; 1000 N s and 1000 kg m/s; 600 and 3750; 500 N; 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 m/s; 300, 400 and 1200 N
No time given: v² = u² + 2as stops a trolley from 0.6 m/s at 0.2 m/s² in 0.36 ÷ 0.4 = 0.9 m, the same as the area under its speed line, ½ × 3 s × 0.6 m/s
Each puzzle offers three answers and accepts only its right one, every wrong answer has its own hint, nothing is marked before Check, and once checked only the right answer is drawn without red
Every demonstration starts after the screen's fade and ends within 5 s of its screen opening; an answer is drawn within 3 s of Check

applied.problem: "Real trolleys also lose a little to their wheels' spin, to any slope" is off: a slope can speed a trolley up as well as slow it, and spinning wheels make it respond as if a little heavier rather than losing momentum.
"The trolley stops 10 s and 2.5 m later" holds only from the opening 0.5 m/s; at the 1 m/s top of the drag it takes 20 s and 10 m, so the figure must be tied to the opening speed.

"It needs one only to make up for friction" is too absolute for the dossier (uphill or into drag it needs more); "A force sets how fast the speed changes" should be the net force; 2000 N to stop in 0.5 s is the average force, not a fixed one.
"Real rolling resistance changes a little with speed and load" understates load: rolling resistance grows roughly in proportion to the load, though only a little with speed.
"A coil has no twin of the third law" is absolute; two coupled coils do act on each other equally (mutual inductance is the same both ways), so the claim should be limited to a single coil.
